title: The serpent's question (Genesis 3:1–7)
hook: did God really say? the fruit, the eyes opened, the fig leaves

segments.voice: Yesterday, ezer: the first not good in the Bible, a person with no one beside them, and your line was bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh.
screen: `BONE OF MY BONES, AND FLESH OF MY FLESH.`

segments.voice: The most dangerous sentences don't always sound like lies. Sometimes they sound like questions. Are you sure your friend meant it that way? Is that really what the doctor told you? A good question opens a door. A twisted one leaves a crack of doubt in something you trusted, and walks away. In the garden, everything is good: two people, side by side, naked and not ashamed. Then, in the third chapter, a new voice arrives. It doesn't start with a command, or a threat. It starts with a question.
screen: `A LIE CAN SOUND LIKE A QUESTION.` → `A CRACK OF DOUBT.` → `A NEW VOICE IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the opening in the King James Bible: "Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?" Look how clever that is. God had said: eat freely of every tree, except one. The serpent turns a whole garden of yes into a single no. And in Hebrew there's a pun. Subtil, crafty, is arum. One verse earlier, the man and woman were arummim, naked. The woman answers, and adds something God never said: neither shall ye touch it. Then the serpent says it plainly: "Ye shall not surely die." The fruit looks good, and pleasant, and wise-making, and she eats, and gives some to her husband, who, the text says, was with her. Then: "the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons." Two things the story doesn't say. It never says apple. That came later; some think a Latin pun helped, since in Latin malum can mean apple, and malum can mean evil. And Genesis never names the serpent as Satan. Christian tradition came to read it that way, following the book of Revelation, which calls the devil that old serpent. Jewish tradition has its own readings of the story. Either way, the text shows how it began: not with a lie, but with a question that bent a good word.
screen: `A GARDEN OF YES BECOMES ONE NO.` · `ARUM AND ARUMMIM: CRAFTY, NAKED.` · `EYES OPENED, FIG LEAVES SEWN.` · `NO APPLE, NO NAME.` · then, large: `YEA, HATH GOD SAID?`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days to a voice, a headline, an ad, a comment, or the one in your own head, that took something good and bent it into a question: did they really mean it? Don't argue with it; just name it for what it is, a question that twists. If you pray, you can hold it up to God.
Arum. The Hebrew word for crafty, used for the serpent, and it sounds just like naked, arummim, one verse before.
Your line: did god really say? A whole garden of yes, and one no. Day three hundred thirty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Some churches read Genesis 3 on the first Sunday of Lent, beside the story of Jesus tempted in the wilderness, where he answers each temptation with words of scripture.

fork.setup: the serpent asks: "yea, hath God said, ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?" you're the woman. what's true?
options: God said eat freely, except from one tree.
fork.reveal: a whole garden of yes, with one no. the question's trick is to make the one no look like everything.

original.note: Hebrew: crafty, shrewd. It echoes arummim, naked, one verse before.

trapdoor: what you thought: the devil, disguised as a snake, tempted Eve with an apple.
what it means: a crafty voice asks a question that bends a good word, and trust cracks.
what a scholar hears: arum and arummim, a pun on crafty and naked; no apple and no Satan in Genesis itself; those come from later reading.
recall: the mark or goal you keep your eyes on
sincere, with no actor's mask on

chat.says: How did the serpent get them to eat the fruit in Genesis?
options: With a question that twisted God's yes to every tree but one into a no.
By forcing them with threats until they were too afraid to say no.
By disguising itself as God and giving them a brand-new command.
chat.meaning: God said eat freely, except from one tree. The serpent's question, hath God said, turned that garden of yes into a single no.

arum.meaning: Hebrew for crafty or shrewd, used for the serpent

arummim.meaning: Hebrew for naked, an echo of arum

malum.meaning: Latin word that can mean apple, and can mean evil

subtil.meaning: old spelling of subtle: crafty, shrewd

Revelation.meaning: the Bible's last book, which calls the devil that old serpent

notes: arum (3:1) / arummim (2:25) wordplay is widely noted; confirm.
Apple and the Latin pun malum/malum: the pun is often suggested; script says 'some think'. Confirm.
Christian identification of the serpent with Satan via Revelation 12:9 and 20:2; Jewish readings described only as 'often read the story differently'. Confirm this is fair and sufficient.
'Many Christian traditions read Genesis 3 at the start of Lent' (howItsDone): e.g. Revised Common Lectionary Lent 1, Year A. Confirm wording.
